title: The Letgo Is a Place
blurb: Dagny holds a dead-still Cob for five minutes against a team that has done this before, and the bell is about to teach her what she didn't know.

blocks.text: The Cob hung dead still above the L4 ledge, and the Saltpan Knockers had stopped trying to move it.

I was on L4 with my right hand on the Pin and my set pointing straight across the shaft at the Knockers' wall. Above me on L3, their Anchor, Joss Pell, had his set pointing straight back at mine. Where his zone and mine overlapped, in the Lap above my head, the two sets cancelled, and the Cob sat there in the lamplight with nothing under it and nothing pulling it anywhere.
Nothing fell in that Lap. Nothing cost either of us a pound. And every count the clock took was one the Ninepins lost, because the Knockers led by a point.

They had pinned Dunnet in the first minute. Pell caught him off his rope and held him flat against our wall for sixty counts, and their Caller sang out the point before Dunnet's boots found the rope again. One to nil. Then the Cob came down into the Lap above me, and I set across to send it at their well, and Pell met me.

I turned. Pell turned with me, a count behind, and the Cob shivered and stayed. I turned back. He came back. Whatever way I pointed, he pointed the other, and he never once looked down at me. He watched the Cob. If I let go, my zone went true down and his set ruled the whole Lap, and his set pointed at our wall. So I held, and he held, and the two of us stood there gripping iron as hard as we could to keep a lump of ore from doing anything at all.

My hand was wet on the Pin. My throat was tight and dry, the way it gets before I'm sick. I counted under my breath, because counting is how I keep the fear out of my fingers. Half a head in the Lap. Nil a minute, because a null costs nothing. Two minutes and forty counts gone. One point down. Every count free to them, and every count gone from us.

And it wasn't truly still. The Cob had come into the Lap with a little push toward our wall, and a null keeps whatever push a thing already has. It was drifting. A hand's width every ten counts, near enough, across the dark toward our side of the shaft.

I knew there was a rule for this. The Letgo. At the five-minute bell, if the Cob is above the L4 ledge floor, every Pin is let go for ten counts. I had read those words in the league book by lamplight at our kitchen table. I knew the words. I didn't know what they would do, and I knew I didn't, and that is a cold thing to know with your hand on a Pin.
"Four minutes," Pru called from the Lip. "Long odds on the far rope, Dunnet. Stay where you are."

Dunnet was on the Knockers' wall rope by L5, where she had sent him to wait for the Cob to come down. It wasn't coming down. Lisbet was on our wall by L2 with the sling coiled over her shoulder. Hal was below me on L6, humming his one low note.

At thirty counts to the bell the Knockers' Dropper came off her rope, swung under the Lap and took hold of our wall rope by L5, one body-length below the Cob. I watched her do it. I didn't know what she was for.
The five-minute bell rang. The Weighman leaned over the Lip rail with his hand up.
"Letgo!"
Then the warning: one ring, two, three. Everyone onto a rope or a ledge. On the first ring I understood it, and the first ring was two rings too late.
Ten counts of true down. The whole shaft straight down, the way it is when nobody is playing. And the Cob had drifted for three minutes on a push nobody stopped. It was hanging over our well.

I did the Release on the warning, because the Release takes three counts and the warning gives you three. Breathe in. Feel the Pin go quiet. Breath and hand together, little finger last. My hand came off the iron.
The Cob dropped.

It went past my ledge close enough that I felt the air move, past Hal on L6, and into our well with a sound like a cellar door slamming. Dunnet was on the wrong side of the shaft. Lisbet was on the wrong ledge. Their Dropper hung on our rope, a body-length from its line. Any of us near the Cob would have found her nearer still.
Four to nil, and the Drop over.

I sat down in the mark. My knees didn't buckle; I just couldn't make them want to stand. Then I counted it again from the beginning, the way you go back over a sum you've got wrong. The pin at one minute bought them the lead. Pell met my set at about two minutes and held it. He never stopped the drift, because the drift was the plan. Their Dropper went to our rope at thirty counts to the bell. Their Caller hadn't said a word for two minutes, because there was nothing left to say. They had timed it to the count. They had done it before. And I had stood under it the whole time and watched them do it, and not known what I was watching.

At the Hoist Lisbet hauled me up in the sling and set me on the Lip planks. The Weighman put me on the scale. I looked for a plumb-bob before I could stop myself. There was none, only the scale and the board and the league book, as the doctor had said.

Before the bell that morning he had booked my carry at nil again, near enough. Two stone of lean-weight sat in my bones by then, two weeks of an ounce an hour, and the book couldn't see a pound of it. Now he wrote nine pounds against my name. My knees said two stone and a half. I stepped off and said nothing, and the saying nothing sat in my stomach like cold porridge.
Lisbet was coiling the far-wall rope beside the shed, fast, without looking at her hands.
"Pru," she said. "Shout the far-wall calls. Don't sign them."
Pru looked up from her chalk board. "I sign them so the Knockers can't—"
"—can't hear them. I know. Let them hear. Shout."
"Their Caller will have every word."
"Then she'll have every word. Shout them."
Pru looked at her a moment longer, flat and plain, the way she is off the shaft. "All right," she said. "Loud."
Osk had been winched to the Lip beside the ladder. He lifted two fingers, and I went and crouched by his chair. Grit ringed its legs. I didn't look at it.

"One," he said, low. "They'll do it again, if they're ahead and it's above L4. Two: the Letgo isn't a bell. It's a place. Where the Cob hangs when it rings is where it goes." He waited, the long wait he takes before the word that matters. "Three. Learn it. Not today. You've no time today."
"I should have known it," I said.
"You should. Now you do."
Walls swapped for Drop 2. We took the odd wall: me on L5, Hal on L3. Pell went up to L2, above Hal, and I think the Knockers meant to catch the Cob high and sit on it again.

Pru shouted every call, loud enough to ring off the Lid. At the bell the Weighman let the Cob go from the centre of the Lid, and Dunnet went off the Lip after it, caught it in his arms and fell with it, straight down through the unheld L1 zone, as fast as true down would take him. Pell could have nulled him in the Lap under his ledge, and it would have done nothing, because a null keeps whatever push a thing already has. Dunnet had all of it. To brake him in his own zone, Pell would have paid two stone a minute for Dunnet's fifteen stone and the Cob. He let him go. Dunnet went through the Lap like a sack through a trapdoor and into Hal's zone, and Hal set it down and across.
"Far rope, L4, Lisbet!" Pru shouted. "Evens it swings to you! Now!"
Lisbet was on our wall, reaching for the far-wall rope end as it came swinging across the shaft to her through the lamplight. It hit her shoulder before her hand found it.
"Bloody hell," she said, and grabbed it on the second swing.

She should have seen that rope coming. It swung into the light a whole count before it reached her. I put it beside the lamp that had burned clean in training week and the arm's length she had missed by, and I left it there, because I didn't want to know what it added up to.

Dunnet came down into my zone with the Cob, and I set L5 across with him, two heads under me, two stone a minute. Twenty counts. I felt every one of them arrive in the bones of my feet. He put it in their well at a minute and fifty. I did the Release, little finger last, and my hand shook coming off the Pin.
Four to three.

At the second Hoist Hal came up the rope on his own, slowly, with a hand pressed to his side between every pull. The Weighman put him on the Lip scale and read it out. Two stone five. He wrote it in the book.
Hal stepped off.

I heard it before I saw it: a breath that stopped halfway. Then he went down onto his knees on the planks, and then onto his side, and he lay there with both arms wrapped round his ribs and his eyes shut tight.

The cold went through the lining of my father's coat first, and then through my hands, so that I couldn't feel my good fingers. I was beside him before I knew I'd moved. My knees hurt when they hit the planks and I didn't care. His face was the colour of chalk. He was breathing in small, short sips, as if a full breath had a knife in it.
"Man down on the landing, Da," I said, under my breath, so that only I could hear it. "Hold the brake."
"Hal," I said. "I'm frightened for you."
"It's not," he said. "Steady. It's not the..." He stopped, because finishing it cost too much.
The Weighman knelt on his other side and put two flat fingers to the ribs, very gently. Hal's whole body went stiff.
"That's an old crack gone through," the Weighman said. "When?"
"Fell," Hal said. "In the yard. Before the..."

"Before the thaw." The Weighman sat back on his heels and looked at the book. "Two stone five on the book today. That's no Crazing. That's a bone you brought with you." He stood up and wrote. "Stood down, Stenning. Till it mends, and till I've had my own hands on it."
Osk said, "Let me see his page."
The Weighman held the book down to the chair. Osk ran one finger down the column without hurrying.
"Left foot at twenty-seven," he said. "Ribs at thirty-one." He looked at me, not at Hal. "Two Crazings. He has one left. This isn't one. The next one is his last."

I thought of Hal on the morning of Match 1, coughing with a hand at his side and taking it away when I looked, and calling me a liability with a cracked rib under his shirt the whole time. He had climbed every rope since then with it. He had held every Pin with it. I had thought he was hard, and he was only hurting and saying nothing, the way I was, and the feeling that came up in my throat then was not anger at all. It was love, and it frightened me as much as his breathing did.
Dunnet stood over us with his big hands hanging. He was white to the lips.
"That Joss Pell," he said, too loud. "Stood so still in Drop 1, the pigeons'll be nesting on him by Thursday."

Nobody laughed. Hal let out one long breath that didn't stop halfway. I was grateful to Dunnet for that, whatever he had taken behind the Lip shed last week, and I hated that I had to think the second thing while I was feeling the first.
The Weighman looked at Pru. "Change, Ninepins?"
"None," Pru said. "We've no reserve that can feel a Pin."
So I went down alone for Drop 3.

We were trailing, so we chose the wall, and I took the odd wall and L5 and left L1 and L3 true down, because one hand holds one Pin and I only had the one. I won't tell Drop 3 as if it were close. I paid for every set I made and I did the Release after every one, and not one hold came near four stone. The Knockers scored at three minutes and twenty, nowhere near any bell. Seven to three.
Our first loss.

On the Lip the Weighman counted crowns into the Knockers' hands and none into ours. Rafe's debt had gone to eighty-eight crowns that morning, and this week nothing went against it. A loss is a week that costs and pays nothing back, and I felt it sitting on top of the stone in my knees, which were nearer five by my own count than four.
Rafe was at the rail. "We'll have them in the return, won't we, Dags?"
"There's no return in the Thaw Round," I said. "We play everyone once."
He went still, and then he nodded, and he didn't joke, and that was worse.

Dunnet and Rafe took the door off the Lip shed and lifted Hal onto it. Hal kept his eyes shut and his jaw tight, and when they raised him he made no sound at all, and that told me more about the pain than any sound would have. They carried him across the Lip toward the gate, slowly, Dunnet at the head and Rafe at the feet, with Lisbet walking beside and holding his hand down flat so it wouldn't knock the frame.
The Weighman wrote one more line in the book, under Hal's name. I read it upside down. STOOD DOWN. BONE.

If Wat Ellery had not walked out of Shaft Nine in his squeaking new boots, there would have been two Anchors left on the Ninepins' register. There weren't. Next Monday the Ninepins would go down the shaft with one Anchor, and the one Anchor was me.
